tasks.title: timeline() reads one page with an indexed query
tasks.summary: Keyset ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT windows replace the whole-table load, parse and sort.
tasks.objective: In factory/orchestrator/src/db/queries.ts, a paged timeline() call (one with a limit) reads its page with keyset windows (`ORDER BY ts DESC ... LIMIT limit + 1`, ascending for an after cursor) and parses only the rows of the windows it reads. Where each filter runs is fixed: (1) In the SQL WHERE: the event-type set `filter.eventTypes ?? timelineEventTypes()`, intersected, when `kinds` is given, with the types whose eventKind is in kinds (eventKind ignores its payload argument, so a kind is a set of event types; this is how the severity-decisions and quorum-decision lens cases move into SQL); the session scope; taskId; and the before/after cursors as an inclusive ts bound against the cursor resolveCursor returns ({ts, eventId}): `ts <= cursor.ts` for before, `ts >= cursor.ts` for after, so the rows that share the cursor's ts reach JS. (2) In JS on raw columns, before any payload parse: the project filter (projectOf); today's cursor filter against that resolved cursor, unchanged (compareLogOrder(e, cursor) < 0 for before, > 0 for after; compareLogOrder lives in factory/orchestrator/src/eventOrder.ts and orders by ts, then session id, then numeric log index); and the ordering of rows that tie on ts with compareLogOrder, so a `#9` event never sorts after a `#10` one. Window order and page order: a before call reads `ORDER BY ts DESC` and its page is, as today, the newest `limit` matching events strictly older than the cursor in compareLogOrder order; an after call reads `ORDER BY ts ASC` and its page is, as today, the oldest `limit` matching events strictly newer than the cursor in compareLogOrder order; both are returned newest-first, as today. Tie groups: a window whose LIMIT is reached reads the rest of the tie group of its last row (the same WHERE, with `ts = lastTs`) before rows are ordered by compareLogOrder and the page is cut, and the next window continues strictly beyond that ts (`ts < lastTs` for before, `ts > lastTs` for after), so no window boundary falls inside a tie group and SQLite's physical order of tied rows never decides which of them a page holds. (3) In JS per window, after the parse, reading further windows until the page plus its more-probe row is full or rows run out: the epic filter (promptInEpic), whose session and named-prompt sets come from one SQL query over the same scoped, project-filtered rows, applying eventTypes but not kinds, because today's epic filter runs before the kinds filter; the query returns each row's task_id column with its payload epic_id and parent_prompt_id extracted by json_extract, parses no payload in JS, and keeps epicOfEntry's precedence: the epic a qualified task id names (through epicOfTaskId) wins, and the payload epic_id counts only when the task id names no epic (null or bare); and the decisions-only lens (applyDecisionsLens), where a dispatch_decision's parent is checked by id lookup against the same filters. (4) After paging, on the page rows only: nearestPromptId (memoized; an ancestor outside the windows read is fetched by id) and the other per-row joins. An unpaged call (no limit) keeps today's load-all path. The paged route's more-probe costs one small window, not a second full query.
